title: Energy spectrum with slope reference: is there an inertial range?
summary: Turbulent kinetic energy per wavenumber on log-log axes with a k to the minus five thirds line for comparison. A straight stretch parallel to the reference is the inertial range; the roll-off at high k is dissipation or grid resolution.

media.alt: Log-log plot of an energy spectrum falling with slope close to minus five thirds, a dashed reference line of that slope, and a steep fall at high wavenumber.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is there an inertial range?
read_the_figure.axes: x: wavenumber k (1/length, here dimensionless, 1 to 300), log scale. y: energy spectrum E(k), log scale from 1e-6 to 1. Dashed orange line: slope -5/3.
look_at: Over which range of k is the solid curve parallel to the dashed line?
Where does the curve bend downwards? That is the end of the inertial range.
How many decades does the straight part cover? A short range means a low Reynolds number.
Is the reference line placed near the data but not on it (to show slope, not level)?
read_the_figure.proves: A band of E(k) that follows the -5/3 slope is the signature of an inertial cascade of energy. It does not prove the flow is fully turbulent isotropic, and the slope alone says nothing about the level.
if_wrong: Steeper than -5/3 right after the large scales: the Reynolds number is too low for an inertial range.
A pile-up before the cut-off: numerical dissipation is not removing energy properly.
No units or no normalisation: the k axis cannot be related to length scales.

terms.meaning: Distribution of turbulent kinetic energy over wavenumber, E(k), so that the integral of E dk is the energy per unit mass.
Spatial frequency, k = 2 pi / wavelength, in 1/m.
Range of scales between the energy-containing and dissipation scales where energy passes down without loss: E = C eps^(2/3) k^(-5/3).
Rate at which kinetic energy turns to heat, eps, in m^2/s^3.
Smallest scale of the flow, eta = (nu^3 / eps)^(1/4).

remember: Inertial range: E(k) = C eps^(2/3) k^(-5/3), C about 1.5.
On log-log axes a power law is a straight line with that slope.
One decade in k lowers E by 10^(5/3) = 46.
The cut-off sits near k eta = 0.1 to 1.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position encodes k (log) and E (log). The solid teal line is the computed spectrum and the dashed amber line is the reference slope. The reference is deliberately offset from the data so that it can be compared by eye as a parallel, not as a fit.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A power law is a straight line on log-log axes and its exponent is its slope. The eye is excellent at judging parallel straight lines, so the -5/3 line turns the question 'is there an inertial range' into 'is there a part of my curve parallel to this line'. The roll-off at the right then shows dissipation, and a bump would show a numerical problem.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What is the slope? From E = 1 at k = 1 to about 0.022 at k = 10 the curve falls by a factor of 46, so the slope is log10(0.022) = -1.66, almost exactly -5/3. Q2: Where does it bend? Near k of 60 to 100 the solid curve drops below the straight continuation: at k = 100 E is about 3e-4 and it plunges to 1e-6 by k = 300. Q3: How wide is the straight part? About two decades in k, from 1 to about 60.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: The -5/3 line and log-log axes: the reference is the test, the axes are what turn a power law into a straight line. Without both there is nothing to compare.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Log-log axes squeeze the plot: a few percent error in slope is hard to see over one decade. The apparent range depends on where the reference line is drawn and how long it is. Smoothing or averaging in bins changes the high-k tail, and a spectrum from a 1D line is not a 3D spectrum. Without the k axis normalised by the scales (k L, k eta), different flows cannot be compared.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A compensated spectrum k^(5/3) E(k) against k, where the inertial range is a flat plateau and deviations are easy to measure. A structure function plot gives the same information in physical space. Spectra of velocity along a line need the one-dimensional constant.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Plot the compensated spectrum below, shade the inertial range, and add a top axis showing the length scale 2 pi / k.

steps.title: Kolmogorov inertial range
steps.note: From dimensional analysis: E has units m^3/s^2, eps m^2/s^3 and k 1/m, and no other scale is available.

steps.title: Slope on log-log axes and the end of the range
steps.note: One decade in k lowers E by a factor 10^(5/3) = 46.4.

worked.title: Where does the inertial range end?
worked.problem: Air with nu = 1.5e-5 m^2/s has dissipation eps = 1 m^2/s^3. Find the Kolmogorov scale and the wavenumber at which the dissipation range starts (k eta = 0.1). Then the fall of E over one decade in the inertial range.
worked.answer: eta = 0.24 mm; the dissipation range starts near k = 415 1/m (wavelength about 15 mm); E falls 46-fold per decade inside the inertial range.

analyze.q: The curve bends at k of 60, well before the grid limit. What physical cause fits, and what numerical one?
Why is the reference line shifted away from the data?
analyze.hint: What does a parallel line show that an overlay hides?

evaluate.q: Is a slope of -1.66 over one decade enough to claim an inertial range?

create: Plot the compensated spectrum k^(5/3) E(k) and mark the plateau.
Add a second spectrum at a higher Reynolds number and see how the range grows.

checks.q: Why draw a line with slope -5/3 on the plot?
checks.hint: Which feature of the data is it testing?
checks.answer: To show whether part of the spectrum is parallel to the inertial-range law.

checks.q: By what factor does E fall over one decade in k if E ~ k^(-5/3)?
The spectrum has a slope of -3 beyond the first few modes. What flow does that suggest?
checks.answer: A steeper slope suggests a low Reynolds number (no inertial range yet) or a 2D or strongly stratified flow, with no -5/3 cascade.
